layout.body:
Jordan Miles
November 3 at 5:37 PM
We're seeking two additional members for our panel at the 2026
Media Studies Conference hosted by
Poplar College.
Please email jmiles@poplar.edu if interested.
Panel title: Rethinking Documentary-
Collaboration and Authorship
Panel description: This panel explores ways to involve participants in documentary production beyond traditional observation. Historically, filmmakers have controlled the narrative, leaving little room for those on camera to shape their own stories.
We' Il discuss methods for working directly with participants to ensure accuracy and trust, providing strategies for scholars and practitioners interested in building stronger partnerships with the communities they document.
Academic Rationale: Recent scholarship emphasizes participatory and community-driven practices as a response to long-standing concerns about representation and authorship. By examining strategies for collaboration, this panel contributes to debates about ethics and methodological innovation in documentary research and production.
Confirmed Participants: Jordan Miles (Moderator), Poplar College; Taylor
Chen, Summit University.

layout.title: Blackout During Finals Week
layout.body:
Blackout Brings
Creativity to Finals Week
A sudden power outage during finals week left Smithfield students scrambling for solutions. Students took advantage f their smart-phone flashlights, and university staff provided camping lights for dorm lounges.
"It was stressful but kind of fun," said sophomore Grace Lee.
The blackout lasted six hours, caused by a transformer failure near campus. Dining services offered free coffee, and professors extended deadlines to ease the pressure.
"We made the best of it," said senior Omar Davis, who studied with his bike light. Social media buzzed with photos of candlelit study sessions, turning the inconvenience into a moment of campus unity.
Some students even organized impromptu acoustic concerts on the quad, proving that creativity thrives under constraints.

Kintsugi, an ancient Japanese art, transforms broken pottery into objects of beauty by highlighting, not hiding, their cracks. Artisans use lacquer mixed with powdered gold, silver, or platinum to repair fractures, creating pieces that often become more valued than their original form.
Originating in the late fifteenth century, kintsugi reflects the philosophy of wabi-sabi, which honors imperfection and transience.
Its message extends beyond ceramics, inspiring personal growth and resilience by advising people t embrace flaws as part of life's narrative. Rather than viewing damage as failure, kintsugi reframes it as transformation, symbolizing strength, authenticity, and renewal in a perfection-driven world.
Today, workshops and studios worldwide teach its technical craft and its profound philosophy, offering learners not only artistic skills but insights into acceptance, individuality, and creative expression. Kintsugi stands as a timeless reminder that beauty lies in uniqueness and in the stories our "cracks" reveal, an idea that applies to academic life and beyond.

layout.title: Why College Students Should Prioritize Sleep
layout.body:
Sleep
College life is a whirlwind of deadlines and social commitments, often causing students to push sleep to the margins.
Yet, restorative sleep iS not optional-it is foundational for cognitive performance and emotional resilience.
Studies link consistent, high-quality sleep to enhanced memory consolidation, sharper focus, and improved problem-solving-skills that underpin academic success. Chronic sleep deprivation disrupts hormonal balance and elevates stress. It even compromises immunity, increasing vulnerability to illness. To safeguard well-being, aim for seven to nine hours of sleep nightly. Establish a regular sleep-wake rhythm, minimize blue-light exposure from screens before bed, and moderate caffeine intake after midday.
While brief naps can alleviate fatigue, they cannot replicate the deep restorative cycles of nocturnal sleep.
Sleep is a strategic investment, not a luxury. Prioritizing rest empowers students to optimize learning, regulate mood, and sustain long-term health, transforming college from a survival sprint into balanced, rewarding experience.

layout.title: AI-Generated Art on Campus
layout.body:
Visitors to the Petrunich Gallery can now view an exhibition of AI-generated paintings that blur the line between human creativity and machine learning. One standout work, Dream Algorithm, depicts a city floating in a sea of binary code, while another, Echoes of Light, uses layered brushstrokes created by artificial neural networks to mimic a sunrise over glass towers.

The exhibit, which was funded by an arts innovation grant, allows visitors to interact with a program that generates custom artwork in real time, allowing them to choose themes and color palettes. This feature has become the centerpiece of the show, enchanting everyone from art majors to computer science instructors.

"We're exploring the intersection of creativity and technology," said curator Dana Fields. "It challenges what art means."

"I made a painting with code—it felt empowering," said senior art major Sofia Ramirez. "It's a new frontier."
